## The questions of the five analysts {#five-analysts-five-questions .smaller}

::: {.fs-70}
| Analyst | Level of analysis in Task 2 | Estimator in Task 2 | Question of the free phase |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 018OL | 420 cells of country, year and wave | random intercepts for country, year and wave | GDP per capita on the mean of the seven positive items |
| KEVF1 | 209,826 respondents | random intercepts for countries and years within countries | GDP growth on the sum of the seven positive items |
| PRL47 | 394,575 respondents | three levels, random slopes, individual and national controls | GDP per capita, growth and a crisis dummy on three positive shares |
| KQXUE | 270 country-years | a fixed effect for each country | GDP growth and unemployment on the cosmopolitan and utilitarian shares |
| **C6HJR** | 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year | GDP growth and unemployment on the share of the seven positive items |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
- Five free analyses, five different questions, and **one shared verdict**, 'evidence for the claim'; three of the five never used the unemployment rate
- Analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions, which is why Lundberg and colleagues ask every study "What is your estimand?" [@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand]
:::

::: {.src}
The record of the robustness study (osf.io/q5h2c) and the public code of the analysts, read on the [background page]({{< var site-url >}}background.html#sec-reanalysts); @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial on the red-card study.
:::

::: notes
Before you write your own estimand, look at what the five of us did in the free first task. One analyst used GDP per capita, another GDP growth, a third GDP measures with a crisis dummy, and three of the five never used the unemployment rate. The outcomes differ as well, a mean, a sum, a share and three separate shares, and so do the units, with two of us on respondents, one on cells of a country in one wave and two on country-years. These are five different questions, and every one of us recorded the same verdict, 'evidence for the claim'. [advance] Auspurg and Brüderl found the same in the twenty-nine teams of the red-card study, where much of what looked like analytical disagreement was unstated disagreement about what was being estimated. Lundberg and colleagues put the remedy in the title of their paper, "What is your estimand?", and that is what you write now.
:::

## The estimand statement {#the-estimand-statement}

::: {.claimcard}
"The expected change in [unit quantity] among [target population] for a 1-percentage-point difference in unemployment, holding [assumptions] fixed."
:::

::: {.small}
- Unit quantity – a *person's* cosmopolitan framing, or a *country-year* mean?
- Target population – which countries, which years?
- Held fixed – the stable traits of a country, the shocks of a year, the other measure of the economy?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Now:** write your one-sentence estimand for the claim in your notes.
:::

::: {.src}
The template follows @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand.
:::

::: notes
Fill in the brackets of the statement on the slide, which gives your estimand for the claim in one sentence. The unit quantity may be the framing of a person or the mean of a country-year, the target population is a set of countries and years, and what you hold fixed may be the stable traits of a country, whatever every country went through in a year, or the other measure of the economy. [advance] Write it down in your notes. Some of you will write about the framing of a person and some about a country-year average, and some will name different years or different things held fixed. None of these statements is wrong, since each asks a different question, in which the coefficient means something different, as in the free analyses of the five of us. Keep your statement for the second half.
:::
